We note that this manuscript addresses the first two questions, while the third question will be the focus of a subsequent manuscript.

Our detailed approach was as follows. First, we summarized exploratory analyses in the discovery datasets into a set of hypotheses that were pre-registered with the aim to be replicated in the replication sample. After posting the pre-registration on OSF, replication analyses were conducted, following the exact same analysis pipeline as described in the pre-registration (and in the earlier paragraph of this Methods section). This included the same exclusion criteria, calculations of behavioral variables, ME-GLM analyses and computational modelling. As pre-registered, we focused on replicating only the analyses that yielded significant findings in the discovery dataset. Furthermore, for clarity, the main text of this manuscript reports the findings that were replicated across the two datasets; and for completeness, the Supplementary Material reports statistics of the findings that did not replicate.

Following the pre-registration, our hypotheses derived from the discovery sample findings were broken down according to our three aims (note, missing numbers correspond to hypotheses that were initially generated but not supported in the discovery sample, so we did not attempt to replicate them in the replication sample).

Characterize decision-making under risk and ambiguity: • H1: Decisions to draw from the urn at baseline are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect), reward probability (>0 effect) and ambiguity (<0 effect).

• H2: Participants are overall risk averse and ambiguity averse.

Characterize decisions to seek social information: • H3: Participants' decisions to seek social information are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect) and reward probability (>0 effect) in risk trials, and reward magnitude (>0 effect) only in ambiguity trials.

• H4a: Participants who are more risk/ambiguity averse seek more information in general.

• H4c: Participants who are more driven by reward during decisions under risk and ambiguity are also more driven by reward when seeking social information. Specifically, the effect of reward probability on information-seeking is positively associated with the effect of reward probability on decisions.

Characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions: • H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.

○ Additional hypothesis from discovery sample finding: social influence is stronger for risky than ambiguous trials • H7: People value their own opinion more than social information • H8: Social influence affects participants' behavior in both risky and safe directions, but there is asymmetry in terms of the direction of behavior under social influence, with stronger influence of the risky vs safe player.

• H9: There is an asymmetry in terms of the direction of behavior under social influence, with stronger influence of the more similar player.

For any null finding to be validated across both discovery and replication datasets, we further performed Bayesian analyses whenever possible, using the BayesFactor package in R, and report the Bayes Factor value BF10 as an index for support in favor of the null hypothesis. BF10 < 0.33 indicates substantial/moderate evidence for the null hypothesis; BF10 < 0.1 indicates strong evidence, and BF10 < 0.01 indicates decisive evidence (Kass & Raftery, 1995).

Results

Drivers of baseline decision-making under risk and ambiguity

Our first pre-registered hypothesis (H1) was that decisions to draw from the urn at baseline are influenced by reward magnitude (positive effect), reward probability (positive effect) and ambiguity (negative effect). We tested this by examining the results of ME-GLMs 1r and 1a. In risk trials (ME-GLM 1r) and in both datasets, both reward magnitude and reward probability had a significant positive effect on the probability of participants choosing to draw from the urn (Fig. 2A-B, Table S1).

Participants' propensity to choose the urn over the coin flip increased with the urn's reward magnitude (Discovery: b = 1.48, t(23610) = 20.17, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.33,1.62]; Replication: b = 1.32, t(22621) = 19.21, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.19,1.46]) and with the urn's reward probability (Discovery: b = 1.41, t(23610) = 22.27, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.28, 1.53]; Replication: b = 1.33, t(22621) = 20.84, p < .001, 95% CI = [1. 20,1.45]).

In ambiguity trials (ME-GLM 1a) and in both datasets (Fig. 2C-D, Table S2), reward magnitude also had a significant positive effect (Discovery: b = 2.91, t(23602) = 16.92, p < .001, 95% CI = [2.57,3.25]; Replication: b = 2.54, t(22633) = 17.25, p < .001, 95% CI = [2.25,2.83]), while ambiguity had a significant negative effect on the probability of participants choosing to draw from the urn, such that people drew from the urn less when its ambiguity increased (Discovery: b = -.69, t(23602) = -15.81, p < .001, 95% CI = [-.77,-.60]; Replication: b = -.62, t(22633) = -14.07, p < .001, 95% CI = [-.71,-.53]).

Our second pre-registered hypothesis (H2) was that participants would be both risk averse (𝜌<1) and ambiguity averse (𝛼>0) overall. One-sample t-tests were performed (i) to compare risk preference 𝜌 from Model 1 to 1, and (ii) to compare ambiguity aversion 𝛼 from Model 1 to 0. Across both datasets, risk preference (Discovery: M = .42, SD = .35; Replication: M = .47, SD = .51) was indeed found to be significantly smaller than 1 (Discovery: t(393) = -32.22, p < .001; Replication: t(377) = -20.58, p < .001; Fig. 2E-F, left). Ambiguity aversion (Discovery: M = .74, SD = .95; Replication: M = .66, SD = 1.08) was significantly greater than 0 (Discovery: t(393) = 15.45, p < .001; Replication: t(377) = 11.93, p < .001; Fig. 2E-F, right). The results suggest overall risk and ambiguity aversion in both samples.

In conclusion, both H1 and H2 were supported by the results and replicated across both datasets.

Reward magnitude and probability drive decisions to seek social information, but ambiguity does not

A novel component of our task is the ability to capture participants' active information sampling decisions, that is whether or not they wanted to see what one or both players chose on each trial. The distribution of these choices across participants is shown in Fig. 3A-B, revealing a general desire to see other players' choices (Discovery mean = .67 ; Replication mean = .66) but also substantial variability (range from 0 to 1 in both datasets).

Our first hypothesis about factors driving these social information-seeking decisions (H3) was that participants' decisions to seek social information would be influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect), reward probability (>0 effect), and ambiguity (>0 effect). We tested this hypothesis by examining the results of ME-GLMs 2r and 2a. In risk trials from the social block (ME-GLM 2r), and in both datasets, both reward magnitude and reward probability had significant positive effects on the likelihood of participants choosing to seek social information from other players (Fig. 3C-D, Table S3). This means that participants were more likely to choose to see other players' choices when reward magnitude was larger (Discovery: b = .33, t(11779) = 8.63, p < .001, 95% CI = [.26,.41]; Replication: b = .27, t(11251) = 7.16, p < .001, 95% CI = [.20,.35]) and when reward probability was higher (Discovery: b = .09, t(11779) = 3.11, p = .002, 95% CI = [.03,.15]; Replication: b = .11, t(11251) = 3.61, p < .001, 95% CI = [.05,.17]). In ambiguity trials from the social block (ME-GLM 2a), reward magnitude also had a significant positive effect (Discovery: b = .35, t(11775) = 7.98, p < .001, 95% CI = [.26,.43], Replication: b = .28, t(11277) = 6.96, p < .001, 95% CI = [.20,.36]), while ambiguity had no effect on the decisions to seek information about others' choices (Discovery: b = .004, t(11775) = .13, p = .90, 95% CI = [-.06,.07], Replication: b = .05, t(11277) = 1.65, p = 0.10, 95% CI = [-.01,.12]) (Fig. 3E-F, Table S4). In other words, partially consistent with H3, and replicated across both datasets, participants' propensity to seek information about other players' choice increased with both reward magnitude and reward probability, but not with ambiguity. Reward probability as a driver of risky choice predicts reward probability as a driver of social information-seeking

We next sought out to examine whether individual differences in baseline attitudes towards reward, risk and ambiguity during decisions predict information-seeking tendencies across participants. This hypothesis (H4) was further broken down into three hypotheses; that participants who were more risk/ambiguity averse would seek more social information in general (H4a), that they would seek more information specifically when uncertainty/ambiguity is high (H4b), and that participants who are more driven by reward during gambling decisions are also more driven by reward when seeking social information (H4c). We also initially hypothesized that participants would seek more information from the partner they are more similar to (H5). We report the findings of H4a in the Supplementary Materials, given that the pre-registered findings did not replicate, while H4b and H5 were not supported in the discovery dataset (see pre-registration for details) and were thus removed from the set of hypotheses to test.

To test H4c, a Pearson's correlation was performed between the effect of reward magnitude on selfblock decisions from ME-GLM 1r, and the effect of reward magnitude on information seeking in social block from ME-GLM 2r. The same analysis was repeated with the effect of reward probability. The effect of reward probability on self-block decisions was positively associated with the effect of reward probability on later information-seeking decisions in the social block (Discovery: r(392) = .13, p = .009, Fig. 4A; Replication: r(376) = .13, p = .015, Fig. 4B). Conversely, the effect of reward magnitude was not correlated between self-block decision and social block information-seeking (Discovery: r(392) = .02, p = .7, Fig. 4C; Replication: r(376) < .001, p = .99, Fig. 4D). This null result was further corroborated by Bayesian correlation analyses providing substantial evidence towards the null hypothesis that the effect of reward magnitude on risky self-choice does not predict how social information-seeking is influenced by reward magnitude (Discovery: BF10 = 0.127; Replication: BF10 = 0.120).

In conclusion, H4c is partially supported by the results: in both datasets, reward probability appears to be driving both decisions under risk and ambiguity and later information-seeking across the same individuals, but reward magnitude does not, and has distinct effects on the two processes. Participants are influenced by others, but value their own opinion more Our final set of hypotheses related to the mechanisms, and individual differences, in social influence, that is how participants' choices in the social block (relative to the self-block) were influenced by the social information they sought from other players.

As a sanity check with previous research on social influence, we first tested whether participants were influenced by other players, and whether that influence applies to both risky and ambiguous trials (H6). We tested this hypothesis by examining the results of ME-GLM 3, which predicted choice during the social block from corresponding past choice during the self block, social information, trial type (coded as ambiguity vs risk) and the interaction between social information and trial type (Fig. 5A-B, Table S5). The main effect of social information was significant in both datasets (Discovery: b = .93, t(23555) = 19.51, p < .001, 95% CI=[.84,1.03]; Replication: b = 1.23, t(22523) = 21.13, p < .001, 95% CI=[1.12,1.34]), suggesting that social information influences participants' decisions in both trial types beyond their own past choices.

We were then interested in the relative weight that people put on their own past choice relative to the social information, with the hypothesis that people value their own opinion more than social information (H7). From the same ME-GLM 3 (Fig. 5A-B, Table S5), in which coefficients were standardized and can therefore be compared, the effect of self-past choice (Discovery: 95% CI = [1.57, 1.77]; Replication: 95% CI = [1.48, 1.70]) was stronger than the effect of social information (Discovery: 95% CI = [.84, 1.03]; Replication: 95% CI = [1.12, 1.34]), as suggested by the nonoverlapping confidence intervals in both datasets. Additionally, the computational parameter ω (Discovery: M = .60, SD = .25; Replication: M = .55, SD = .26) was found to be significantly greater than 0.5 in a one-sample t-test and in both datasets (Discovery: t(393) = 7.49, p < .001; Replication: t(377) = 3.69, p < .001), suggesting that in the computational model, self-past choice was also weighted more strongly than social information during decisions in the social block (Fig. 5C-D). In conclusion, both H6 and H7 were supported by the results and replicated across both datasets. between SocialInfo and trialType. This allowed testing for the overall presence of social influence regardless of trial type (H6) and for overweighing of individual versus social information (H7). Plotted are box plots of random effects for each ME-GLM predictor, in the discovery (A) and replication (B) datasets, dots represent individual random effects for each participant, blue * denote significant fixed effect (p<0.05), purple * denotes significant differences between effects of standardized predictors (non-overlapping 95% confidence interval). C-D. H7 confirmation with computational modelling: Participants weigh their own past choice more than social information. Plotted are box plots for best-fitting ω parameter estimates from Model 2, for both discovery (C) and replication (D), representing the weight of self versus social information and bounded between 0 and 1, with 0.5 reflecting equal weight. Dots represent individual parameter values, * denote significant t-test (p<0.05) comparing the weight parameter to 0.5.

Social influence asymmetry between risky and safe players

Related to the novel insights in the mechanisms of social influence on decisions under risk and ambiguity, we predicted that social information would influence participants' behavior in both risky and safe directions, but that there would an asymmetry in terms of the direction of social influence, with stronger influence of the risky vs safe player (H8). We tested this hypothesis by examining the results of ME-GLM 4, which predicted choice in the social block from past self-block choice on the same trial design, as well as social information from the safe partner and social information from the risky partner as separate, standardized predictors. We found a significant positive effect of information from both the risky player (Discovery: b = .89, t(23556) = 23.09, p < .001, 95% CI=[.81,.96]; Replication: b = 1.01, t(22524) = 21.00, p < .001, 95% CI=[.91,1.10]) and the safe player (Discovery: b = .19, t(23556) = 6.88, p < .001, 95% CI=[.14,.24]; Replication: b = .60, t(22524) = 16.65, p < .001, 95% CI=[.53,.67]), confirming that participants' choice is influenced in both directions (Fig. 6A-B, Table S6). Additionally, the non-overlapping confidence intervals indicate that the risky player's choice has a stronger influence than the safe player's choice, suggesting asymmetry in social influence. Our computational modelling parameter 𝛾 from Model 2 corroborated these findings. Specifically, the weight of risky versus safe influence 𝛾 (Discovery: M = 1.17, SD = .36; Replication: M = 1.11, SD = .36) was found to be significantly greater than 1 in a one-sample t-test (Discovery: t(393) = 9.60, p < .001; Replication: t(377) = 5.67, p < .001; Fig. 6C-D), which further confirms that in both datasets information from the risky player is weighted more strongly than information from the safe player. Note that the asymmetry parameter 𝛾 shared less than 2% of variance with the individual vs social influence weight parameter ω (Discovery: R=-0.11, shared variance R² =0.012; Replication: R=-0.079, shared variance R² =0.0062), suggesting that the two processes captured by these parameters are dissociable. Finally, we were interested in testing one last hypothesis pertaining to how individual differences in baseline decision-making might relate to this asymmetry in social influence. Our prediction was that the more similar player would have a stronger influence on participants' choices, such that those participants who are generally risk/ambiguity averse would be more influenced by the safe player (who is also more generally risk/ambiguity averse), while those who are more risk/ambiguity seeking would be more influenced by the risky player (H9). To test this hypothesis, Pearson's correlations were performed between the composite measure of aversion 𝜌𝛼 and the difference in social influence from the risky versus safe player from ME-GLM 4, as well as between 𝜌𝛼 and the 𝛾 parameter from Model 2 (see Fig. 7A-B for a summary of all correlations). We reasoned that 'riskier' individuals (i.e.

individuals with lower aversion parameters) would be more strongly influenced by the risky player, therefore resulting in a negative correlation. This is indeed what we found (Fig. 7C-D): the composite aversion parameter 𝜌𝛼 was negatively correlated with 𝛾 (Discovery: r(392) = -.28, p < .001, Fig. 7C; Replication: r(376) = -.16, p = .002, Fig. 7D). Whether this association was driven specifically by risk or ambiguity aversion was less clear. In the discovery sample, the association appeared to be driven by ambiguity aversion (α & γ, r(392) = -.23, p < .001, Fig. 7A), but not by risk preference (ρ & γ, r(392) = .09, p = .09). In the replication sample, however, this dissociation was not replicated, since ambiguity aversion did not significantly correlate with the safe vs risky asymmetry parameter (α & γ, r(376) = -.09, p = .09). Therefore, our findings are consistent with an overall role of combined aversion rather than a specificity towards risk or ambiguity, such that participants with high combined risk/ambiguity aversion are less likely to be influenced by the risky player and/or more likely to be influenced by the safe player. In conclusion, both H8 and H9 were supported by the results and replicated across both datasets. 641 Discussion 642

In this study, we examined social decision-making under risk and ambiguity by separating three 643 processes that are often studied independently: individual baseline valuation of uncertain options, 644 active sampling of social information, and integration of sampled social information into subsequent 645 choice. Across a discovery sample and an independent pre-registered replication sample, we found 646 that social information-seeking was driven by reward magnitude and probability, but not by ambiguity; 647 that social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices while being weighted less 648 strongly than participants' own prior choices; and that social influence was asymmetric, with choices 649 from a risky partner exerting stronger influence than choices from a safe partner. We further showed 650 that this risky/safe asymmetry varied with baseline risk/ambiguity aversion, suggesting that individual 651 valuation tendencies shape selective susceptibility to social influence. Together, these findings 652 support a multi-process account in which social decision-making under uncertainty emerges from 653 distinct but related mechanisms of valuation, social sampling, and social integration. For 654 completeness, our pre-registered hypotheses, and corresponding findings in two independent 655 samples, are summarized in H4c: Participants who are more driven by reward during decisions under risk and ambiguity are also more driven by reward when seeking social information. Specifically, the effect of reward probability on information-seeking is positively associated with the effect of reward probability on decisions.

Supported Supported samples.

Characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions

There are two key differences between our paradigm and the literature on uncertaintydriven information-seeking that could explain our lack of finding. First, uncertainty in the existing literature is usually measured from a known gamble probability (gamble variance, or how close the outcome probabilities are to the highest uncertainty of 0.5), a learned outcome probability (from bandit-type tasks), or subjectively reported uncertainty (questionnaire, confidence rating scale). Therefore, this raises the possibility that uncertainty reduction dominates over ambiguity reduction as a motive to seek information. Second, and perhaps most importantly, the information being provided in our study is social information -meaning what option was chosen by one or two other playersrather than resolving the urn and/or providing outcome information. Therefore, the nature of the information may matter, with social information in our task not actually reducing uncertainty or ambiguity. Future studies should actively manipulate and/or measure uncertainty and ambiguity to clearly separate their influence on information-seeking decisions, as well as to understand how people perceive a reduction in uncertainty and/or ambiguity when exposed to different types of information, specifically social versus outcome information.

Social influence can be decomposed into overall social weighting and risky/safe asymmetry

A second contribution of our study is that it separates two components of social influence that are often conflated: overall susceptibility to social influence (relative to reliance on individual valuation only) and asymmetric weighting of different sources of social information. Prior work has provided mixed evidence about whether social influence is stronger in risky or safe direction. In late childhood and adolescence, safe advice has sometimes been found to exert a stronger influence than risky advice (Blankenstein et al., 2016; Braams et al., 2019; Ciranka & van den Bos, 2019), whereas in later adolescence and adulthood, this asymmetry might reverse, with individuals becoming less sensitive to safe social information, and risky social information exerting stronger influence (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025). Our findings, related to hypothesis #8, extend this literature by testing for a slightly different asymmetry, namely not which kind of information has the strongest influence, but which kind of social partner. We show that the risky partner exerted stronger influence on participants' choices than the safe partner, extending the asymmetry from social information (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025) to social partners, and suggesting that in adulthood, sensitivity to risky influence is heightened compared to safe influence. Future work will be needed to assess whether the developmental trajectory highlighted in past work also applies to social partner-driven asymmetry, rather than social information.

Additionally, we found that social information influenced choices regardless of trial types, suggesting that the impact of others' choices generalizes across both risk and ambiguity trials -or known and unknown form of uncertainty, in line with Braams et al. (2019). However, evidence that social influence differed in strength between risky and ambiguous choices was not robust across samples.

Our computational modelling analyses further clarify the mechanistic structure of social influence during decisions under risk and ambiguity. Previous research has modeled social influence in several ways, including as changes in subjective value (Chung et al., 2015) possibly combined with heuristics (Orloff et al., 2024), changes in risk preference (Braams et al., 2021), or changes in belief about the probability distribution of the prospects (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025). Our goal was not to adjudicate between these possible mechanisms, but to ask whether overall reliance on social information can be dissociated from asymmetric weighting of risky versus safe social partner. Consistent with evidence for egocentric discounting found in past studies (Puskaric et al., 2017; Schöbel et al., 2016; Yaniv & Kleinberger, 2000), we show that participants weighted their own preferences more strongly than social information. However, social influence was not captured solely by this overall social-vs-self weighting: our model also accounted for the asymmetry between safe and risky social influence with a separate parameter. Previous work formally modelling this asymmetry (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2019 , 2025) has assumed that social influence was driven by separate social sensitivity parameters when the social information is risky compared to when it is safe, yielding the risk that while the two parameters might differ from one another to index the asymmetry, they also likely share a lot of variance that reflects overall susceptibility to social influence. Our model is able to better parametrize and dissociate the two cognitive processes, in addition to modelling ambiguity and risk aversion during baseline choices: an overall social sensitivity parameter (ω), and the asymmetric integration of information from the risky vs safe social partner (𝛾). These two parameters were only weakly correlated, sharing less than 2% of variance, thus capturing two key aspects of social influence under risk and ambiguity and indicating that social sensitivity and risky/safe asymmetry capture distinct components of social influence under uncertainty. Such asymmetries in social influence may extend beyond other domains than risky and ambiguous decision-making, as evidenced by a recent study showing that during social contagion of cheating, dishonest social influence was stronger than honest social influence (Benistant et al., 2026). This underscores the importance of better characterizing these asymmetries and their relationships across domains and across the sources of influence (e.g., information versus partner).

Baseline decision-making tendencies shape asymmetric social influence

A third contribution of the present study is that it shows how individual valuation tendencies shape later social influence. Risk and ambiguity attitudes at baseline varied substantially across participants (Fig. 2E-F), as did social information-seeking (Fig. 3A-B) and the parameters capturing self-versussocial weighting (Fig. 5C-D) and risky/safe asymmetry (Fig. 6C-D). This heterogeneity allowed us to test whether baseline decision-making tendencies predict how people subsequently sample (hypothesis #4) and integrate (hypothesis #9) social information.

Hypothesis #4 was only partially supported. Specifically, we did not find replicated support for the prediction that risk/ambiguity averse individuals would seek more social information overall (H4a, only supported in the discovery sample), possibly because the distribution of individual propensities to seek information was heavily skewed (Fig. 3A-B). However, we found in both samples that people's sensitivity to reward probability during baseline decisions translated into similar sensitivity when deciding to seek social information (H4c), suggesting that sensitivity to reward probability may generalize across different decision domains; specifically, here, value-based decisions and social information-seeking decisions. This finding contributes to a better understanding of how informationseeking processes, usually ignored from standard cognitive ontologies (Poldrack & Yarkoni, 2016), relate to other forms of decision-making. Finally, hypothesis #9 was also supported in both samples, with the asymmetric social influence of the safe versus risky partner found to depend on individuals' baseline risk/ambiguity aversion. This association was such that individuals with lower baseline aversion (i.e. more inclined to take risks) also displayed a stronger asymmetry and were more influenced by the risky player. Overall, this finding is consistent with other studies (Chung et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2016), indicating greater susceptibility to influence from similar partners, whose choices align with one's own baseline preferences.

Although the present manuscript focuses on links among cognitive processes within the task, this heterogeneity may also inform future work on linking these processes to transdiagnostic symptom dimensions relevant to autism and social anxiety; since both have been related to risk aversion, ambiguity aversion, and social influence (Chamberlain et al., 2013; Chevallier et al., 2012; Fujino et al., 2017; Hedger et al., 2020; Lee & Chung, 2022; Sandhu et al., 2023). With the heterogeneity of participants' decision-making mechanisms evidenced here, future research can explore whether variation in social information-seeking or asymmetric risky vs safe social influence may help dissociate symptom dimensions relevant to autism and social anxiety, which are often co-occurring.

Limitations

The current study has several limitations worth noting. First, the study design generally treated choosing the urn as the riskier behavior. The risky partner in the social block was programmed to choose from the urn more than the safe partner, with this tendency generated by differences in the two partners' risk and ambiguity aversion parameters. However, in practice, the urn was not always the riskier option given that the alternative coin flip option also involved uncertainty, with a fixed 50% chance of a smaller reward. To mitigate this limitation, we avoided labeling the options simply as "risky" and "safe" throughout this manuscript, and instead labelled and analyzed choices as "drawing from the urn" with "flipping the coin". Future designs could include decision options that more cleanly separate riskiness from reward magnitude, probability and ambiguity.

Second, there were only two partners for whom risk and ambiguity attitudes were confounded, i.e. the safe partner had both high risk aversion and high ambiguity aversion and the risky partner had both low risk and ambiguity aversion. Some previous literature, as well as our baseline decision-making model, has dissociated the effect of risk aversion from ambiguity aversion. People were found to be more averse to ambiguity than risk (Vives & FeldmanHall, 2018), and social influence was found to occur primarily through changes in risk, but not ambiguity attitudes (Braams et al., 2021). To better dissociate social influence on risk versus ambiguity attitudes, future studies could include a larger set of partner profiles in which risk and ambiguity preference vary independently.

Finally, the current study used an online task in which participants were not paired with live partners, and partners' responses were pre-programmed. Although the instructions of the social block stated that participants would observe previously recorded partners' decisions, some participants may nevertheless have suspected that partner choices were simulated, and effects may have been larger in a naturalistic live interaction. Future work can improve ecological validity by using live partners or administering the task in-person, also increasing the generalizability of the findings to real life. Including other factors that affect social information-seeking and social influence such as social knowledge (how much information one has about the partners), familiarity, perceived partner honesty, and demographic similarity, would also be of interest.

Contributions and conclusions

The present study advances a multi-process account of social decision-making under risk and ambiguity. Rather than treating individual valuation, social information-seeking and social influence as independent, unrelated processes, we measured them within the same individuals and quantified their underlying mechanisms and relations using behavioral analyses and computational modelling. Our findings make three theoretical and replicated contributions: social information-seeking was sensitive to stakes rather than ambiguity; social influence could be decomposed into overall susceptibility and risky/safe partner asymmetry; and baseline risk/ambiguity aversion shaped asymmetric social influence. Methodologically, our study combines a discovery-confirmation design with pre-registered replication in two large independent samples, as well as parsimonious computational models that capture baseline decision-making and social influence decomposition. Together, the present findings support our proposal that social decision-making under uncertainty emerges from the combination of individual valuation, active social information sampling, and selective integration of others' choices. This framework paves the way for future investigations further characterizing how these processes relate to other cognitive and social learning constructs as well as to mental health symptoms.

Table 1: Summary of pre-registered hypotheses and findings in the discovery and replication samples.

Note that hypotheses not shown (e.g. H5) were not supported in the discovery sample and were therefore not included in the pre-registered replication analyses.

Social information-seeking reflects motivational salience, but not ambiguity reduction

First, we found that participants' decisions to seek information from other people, namely to see the decisions of (up to) two other players, were driven by the expected reward probability and magnitude of the varying decision option (the urn). This suggests that when the varying option is more motivationally salient -because possible rewards are larger or, in risk trials, more probable -people are more likely to want to know what other people did. This pattern of information-seeking is consistent with a growing body of literature showing that, even when information is non-instrumental (i.e. cannot be used to alter choices), people are biased towards seeking desirable information (Charpentier et al., 2018; Charpentier & Dezza, 2022; Jiwa et al., 2023; Kelly & Sharot, 2021; van Lieshout et al., 2021). Here, we extend this idea to a different kind of information and to social contexts: instead of the information being about the outcome of an uncertain lottery, it is about knowing the choices made by other people. The information is not valenced per se in this task, since seeing the other players' choice doesn't directly convey information about the outcome of the lottery. Additionally, the social information could be considered instrumental, since participants can use it to alter their choice later on -even though it wouldn't increase their odds. One possible interpretation is that participants sought social confirmation or anticipated agreement, both of which are desirable and socially rewarding forms of information (Kappes et al., 2020; Mistry & Liljeholm, 2019). That is, when stakes are high, participants may be more motivated to know whether others made the same choice, and in doing so increase the likelihood that the social information will confirm their choice. Whether driven by expected value or anticipated social validation, these findings are consistent with motivational salience as a key driver of social information-seeking.

On the other hand, contrary to our predictions, we did not find ambiguity to be a significant predictor of social information-seeking. Previous research suggests that information is often sought to reduce uncertainty (Charpentier et al., 2018; Gershman, 2019; Kelly & Sharot, 2021; van der Sluis, 2025; van Lieshout et al., 2021; White et al., 2019), so ambiguity as a form of unknown uncertainty was predicted to increase people's desire to see other people's choices. Yet, we did not observe an effect of ambiguity on the decision to seek social information, and this null effect was robust across the two Supplementary Material

Self-report questionnaires

Fifteen self-report questionnaires were administered to assess symptom dimensions relevant to psychopathology: State/Trait Anxiety Inventory (Spielberger, 1983), Intolerance to uncertainty (IUS, (Carleton et al., 2007), 10-Item Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen, 1988), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II, (Beck et al., 1996), Social Responsiveness Scale 2 (SRS-2-SR; (Constantino & Gruber, 2012), 10-item Autism Quotient (AQ10; (Allison et al., 2012)), Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS, (Liebowitz, 1987), Social Curiosity Scale (Renner, 2006), Attributional complexity (Fletcher et al., 1986), Compliance scale (Gudjonsson, 1989), Social Network Index (Cohen et al., 1997), Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory (OCI-R; (Foa et al., 2002), Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire -brief revised (SPQ-BR; (Davidson et al., 2016), Barratt Impulsiveness (BIS-11; (Patton et al., 1995). There were 8 catch questions in total in the 15 questionnaires to make sure participants paid attention.

Analyses and findings related to these questionnaires are not reported in the current manuscript as they are outside the scope of the proposed research questions, and will be the focus of a future manuscript.

H4a: Participants who are more risk/ambiguity averse seek more information in general.

A Pearson's correlation was performed between ρα and the propensity to seek information from at least one player. The aversion composite measure was positively correlated with information-seeking in the discovery sample, r(392) = .12, p = .02. We then explored the correlation between risk and ambiguity parameters and information-seeking separately. ρ was negatively correlated to informationseeking, r(392) = -.10, p = .04, but α was not, r(392) = .04, p = .46. Higher aversion, especially higher risk aversion, was correlated with a higher propensity to seek social information. However, the correlation between ρα and social-information seeking was not significant in the replication sample (r(376) = .01, p = .79)

H6: Additional finding from ME-GLM 3: social influence is stronger for risky than ambiguous trials.

There was also an interaction between social influence and trial type in the discovery sample (b = -.21, t(23555) = -5.16, p < .001, 95% CI=[-.30,-.13]), suggesting that social influence is stronger for risk than ambiguity trials. However, this effect was not significant in the replication sample (b = 0.02, t(22523) = 0.44, p = 0.66, 95% CI=[-.07,.11]).

H8: Additional analysis comparing choice propensity between blocks. 1033

Anecdotally, we also found in the Discovery sample that the probability of drawing from the urn was 1034 also lower in the self (M = .45, SD = .18) than in the social block (M = .48, SD = .19), t(393) = -4.52, p 1035 < .001, suggesting an overall shift towards more risky behavior. However, this finding was not 1036 replicated in the Replication sample (self block: M = .46, SD = .18; social block: M = .47, SD = .18), 1037 t(377) = -1.06, p = .29. While pre-registered, we note that this test was not an appropriate test of 1038 social influence since it's very unspecific -several factors, such as practice or time effects, could 1039 explain the shift between blocks besides social influence. Additionally, as acknowledged in the 1040 discussion, drawing from the urn isn't necessarily the "riskier" choice, since flipping the coin also 1041 incurs a risk. Thus, we consider this analysis to be irrelevant in assessing support for H8; the main 1042 analysis supporting H8 is presented in the main text. 1043 1044 Supplementary Tables 1045 Table S1.

Figure S1.

Parameter recovery. To validate our computational models, we performed parameter analyses using participants' best-fitting parameters from the discovery sample (N=394) to generate data using each Model. Models were then re-fit to the generated data using the same optimization method as for the main model-fitting analyses. Parameter estimates from the recovery were correlated with the actual parameters used to generate the data, for both Model 1 (A) and Model 2 (B). Each scatter plot depicts the recovery of a single parameter, described in the plot title. Each dot is a participant, red lines show the best-fitting line, dashed blue lines are the identity line. R: Pearson's correlation coefficient, p: P-value from the two-tailed correlation test.
